projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Eugene M. Laubach was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Eugene M. Laubach. Mr. Laubach served in the U.S. Army with the 3198th Signal Service Battalion. He served in the China Burma India Theater and his highest rank was T-4. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Laubach's home in Mentor, Ohio on January 17th, 2003. Eugene was seventy-seven at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Little Rock, Arkansas. My hometown.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you? Tell me when you were born and I'll do the math.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Twenty-five. Sixteen I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were sixteen. So you were probably still in high school?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. In fact I was sitting in the dining room at home listening to some symphony that came out of New York City every Sunday and I heard John Charles Thomas or whatever his name was, the narrator, we interrupt this program to tell you and away we went. Me and fifteen million others. In other words he was announcing Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now did any of your classmates even though they might have been under age, did any of them quit school, lie about their age and try to enlist?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Rush out and enlist? I can't remember. I don't really know though.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Fools rush in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: My two brothers both of which are older than I, I'm the baby of the family. I'm only seventy-seven. They were both in the National Guard and had graduated from high school. And the National Guard was an anti-aircraft battalion was, and a lot of them if not all, were federalized in January of '41. And they were sent to Fort Bliss, Texas and in August of 1941 they went overseas. My two brothers, their battalion that is, wound up in Dutch Harbor, Alaska. Nice place I guess, but not from what I heard. Well, I didn't think my place was so good where I wound up, but to each his own. And so I graduated from high school, I didn't rush into it because I knew they were coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you involved in any kind of scrap drives or any kind of war related things when you were still in high school before you went in?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: God, my memory is good but it's short. I don't remember. Might have, but I don't really recall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So then you were drafted.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. I filled out the questionnaire that they gave you. You sent it in and less than a week later back came a questionnaire, bang -- or may be redundant but anyway I signed the necessary papers, came back a questionnaire, filled it out, sent it in and ticky-tocky ticky-tocky, see I was born in October. I sent it in and many, many moons went by. But prior to that I was, after I got out of high school I got a job luckily because most industries didn't want to hire short timers and they knew high school graduates were bye-bye most likely. But I got a job, and then I got a letter one day from the American Red Cross which struck me as funny when I read it. They said they want me to come down and talk to them and tell them what I would like to do in the Army and why, or what branch of service in other words. Well, why not? So I did. I told them I wanted to go, I would like to go into the Signal Corps, get some experience in communications because I was thinking about taking that in college. Now I did not go into college after I graduated from high school because you were getting yanked out and why bother, lose all your money. So I didn't. So I went and talked to the Red Cross and that's the last I thought of it until many years later. Well, in January I guess it was of '42, '44 excuse me, I graduated in '43. I'm going the wrong direction. I got a draft notice to report on such and such a date in February. It happened to be the 14th of February and I thought that was a hell of a Valentine's Day gift. And I still remember the way the letter starts. Greeting. Your friends and neighbors have selected you to represent them in one of the branches of the Armed Forces of the United States. And I'll say no friend or neighbor of mine would have done that to me. But anyway moving right along, I was inducted and went in the service, active service on the 14th of February at Camp Robinson in Arkansas which was in North Little Rock, right across the river. But I sat there and twiddled my thumbs for quite a while. Then all of a sudden I got orders to report to Camp Crowder, Missouri, going to Camp Crowder, Missouri which is Signal Corps. Well, unfortunately I came down with strep throat and wound up in the army hospital there I won't say a week, but a period of time. I thought well, that's that. I ain't going to the Signal Corps. I'll be a gravel cruncher. Infantry. Well I came back out of the hospital and I sat around and sat around and sat around doing whatever they told me to do, peel these potatoes or so forth. And lo and behold along come another shipment of GIs up to Camp Crowder, Missouri. The Signal Corps. So I went. I don't know how that was arranged, but many years later I wonder if my father had something to do with that whole thing. The Red Cross. Because he knew every politician in town, the U.S. Senators and Representatives, he dealt with lawyers and everything else. He was not a lawyer. So I wonder if he had pulled some strings. I never knew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You never talked with him about that?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No. For some reason I just did not. But I didn't. So I sent in the Signal Corps at Camp Crowder, Missouri and took my basic training there and my advanced training. Then lo and behold as everything goes I got placed on a troop train and went west as Forest Greeley said. Not for the same reason. Wound up at Camp Beaver ,California which was a repo depot, replacement depot. And I was not assigned to any particular company or battalion. I was just a replacement like everybody up there was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your specific job at that point?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well I had been trained as a lineman repairman, telephone telegraph repairman I should say. And so at that particular time after we left the base of, finished advanced training you were just doing what they told you to do. Nothing. I had no particular assignment. I was just waiting which is the normal thing that happens in the army when nothing is going on. So eventually we got orders to pack up and head to the rail side inn on a given day in January '45. And we marched in parade formation and a big band in front of us. Got over to the rail side inn at Camp Beale California and lo and behold there was pullmans and my heart sank because pullmans means you're going to be on that train a long time, several days. And some of the guys from Camp Beale have been in pullmans, they wound up going to Europe and might have been called up in the Bulge or who knows. Well, didn't work that way. We went south. Got up the next morning and there we were in the Long Beach, California area. And so after a couple of days aboard ship we went. The US General CG Morton. I'll never forget that creaky old thing because I spent forty-two, count them, forty-two days on that thing. Going across the south Pacific of Australia and up to Calcutta, India.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do to pass the time?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well, for a long time you, between breakfast and the evening meal which you only got two meals a day unless you were on a working pardon. And sometimes to past the time you listened to your stomach growl at you because I'm hungry. The only time, if you were on a working detail you got the third meal. And there was an old adage in the army never volunteer for anything because you might regret it. Well there is a bit of truth in that. But one day they asked for volunteers because they needed some people and I stuck my hand up, I'm going to get to eat, I don't care what the detail is. I lucked out and what I wound up doing was in the serving galley, serving food. Couldn't beat that job. So forty-two days after we sailed out of Long Beach, California with a stop at Pearl Harbor and bottom of Australia, Millwood. We wound up in beautiful Calcutta. Went up the Hugli River. Got barged over to the shore because the ship grew too much water. The piers there on the Hugli River wasn't deep enough so we got barged over and wound up in Cancpera, India which is about twenty-eight miles northeast of Calcutta. And I don't know now how long I spent there. We sailed out of Long Beach in January and forty-two days later, blah, blah. And then sit around twiddle your thumbs, twiddle your thumbs, and to pass the time I wound up on a temporary duty in the quarter master quarter passing out uniforms to guys that just come off the ship. The uniforms for replacements and this, that, and the other. Because at that time you did not have to pay for your uniforms. They were gratis. Now I understand and for many years you have to pay for your uniforms, but you get an allowance I understand. But then now just a guy needed a new pair of khakis, what size. I was just, you know, passing time til a bunch of us finally got our orders as replacements to go to beautiful Bhamo, Burma. B-h-a-m-o. Lovely place. And so away we went. Took the Bangle of Samaray up to Leedo, India which was up in the tea country and this was the head of the Leedo Burma Road. It was called Leedo Burma Road or sometimes the Stillwell Road because when the Japanese invaded Burma they cut off the Burma Road that started down in Ragoon, anyway. And so the US Corps of Engineers built this new road out of Leedo, India down through the Himalayan Foothills down to some spot in Burma where they joined the old Burma Road. And so I wound up down there until we got ordered to move to China. And then I got assigned to fly up from Bhamo Burma to Leedo India to pick up army trucks to stash our gear in. So away we went and drove down from Leedo to India to Bhamo Burma and that took, I don't know, maybe seven to ten days. You didn't get very much mileage, distance in those days. Not because the trucks weren't any good, because the hills were sort of vertical in a lot of places. But there were a lot of flat places along the Irrawaddy River where Bhamo was, but up the northern parts of India and Burma it was mountainous and then you would get valleys like you would most any place. But I made two trips up to Leedo India to pick up trucks and then after we got back from the second trip we had enough trucks to load all the gear on. Transmitters, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And away we went on the third leg of the Burma Road which was interesting because from Leedo India to about Bhamo or just a little south of Bhamo Burma the semis could run on the road. But from there on the grades got too steep so everything was put into what were called at that time the old army six buy. And from there on we trudged up through the Himalayans, across the Salween River, and that was an experience because we came down this real steep hill to the Salween River approaching the river and here was a suspension bridge. And we got down there and there was a Chinese guard allowing only one truck at a time on the bridge. I didn't understand why but I found out. When my turn came I drove onto the bridge, the front wheels got on the wooden, there were wooden planks, don't ask me how thick, strung horizontally across. And fine and dandy, I got the rear wheels on all the way to that truck I had the bridge floor in front of me jump high. I thought the bridge had broken and it scared the living daylights out of me. Because the Salaween River at that time was close to flood stage and if you had gone into that river it would have been bye-bye. But what happened, the weight caused it to do that and as you progress across it you just iron out that field in front of you. And then we crossed over and went up on the other side and I put - the trucks at that time had a throttle on them, you pull it out. I put it in front wheel drive so I had six wheels driving and the throttle pulled all the way out and I made zero miles per hour on the speedometer. It took me a long time to get across. And when I got up at the top I looked down and here were the little toy soldiers and toy trucks. Just like you buy, what's those little cars that the kids buy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Matchbox.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: That's the ones. They looked like matchboxes. And they were very steep. And what I was driving at that time was a truck loaded with teakwood. Don't ask me why. I think a little politics, they wanted teakwood in China and the teakwood forest in Burma. So we got teakwood logs and lumber.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Furniture or building? You don't know what they wanted it for.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I don't know what they wanted. Or a hell of a lot of butcher blocks. I don't know. I never saw it again after I got to Kunming, China, which is the end of the Burma Road. And before we got there, it was down towards the end of World War II, the rumors were running around rampant and we heard them because in the Signal Corps we had all sorts of radio equipment to receive it. And so rumors were running rampant, the war is over, the war is over. Well you know how rumors go. Most of them are not true. Well one night after hearing several of the rumors I laid down in the truck cab. Now we are somewhere in China on the Burma Road and I laid down on the truck seat to go to sleep. And somewhere during the night some guy came running down the cover, the war is over, the war is over, the war is over. And it wasn't. I could have killed him though because I was dreaming that I was six blocks from home and getting ready to go home and just about six blocks away he woke me up. And I wasn't six blocks from home. I was on the other side of the world. I could have killed the guy. Fortunately I never found him. But that's one of those funny side of things you run into. Other things weren't quite so funny but there were, a lot of them are, weren't then but in retrospective, you know how that goes. Like one night we're sitting there and the monsoons over there it rains like the devil, around four hundred and sixty inches a year in roughly a six month sphere and that's a lot of water. And the Burma Road wasn't paved. It was just plain old mud in the monsoon season. And when it was dry it was a dust bin. But one night I strung my jungle hammock between the bumper of the truck in front of me and the back bumper of my truck and climbed in and went to sleep. And sometime during the middle of the night I must have rolled over rather strenuously because one of the supports broke and I wound up in the mud. (laughs.) I can laugh now but I didn't laugh at the time. I survived it in spite of myself. But we eventually got into Kunming and we were temporarily belotted in an abandoned rice patty outside of Kunming. And so we just, well sat around twiddle thumbs until they tell you what they are going to do. And part of the battalion was in the town of Kunming in you might call it barracks, single story barracks made out of wood and the roof was slate or something and a garrison with a wall around him and guards at the entrance. But the other part of it a bunch of us were out there in tents which was all right, we didn't have to wade through the muddy rice. But I went into Kunming one evening and there were two or three of us and we were standing there on the street corner rubbernecking. And this at 5, 6 o'clock in the evening, merchants were shutting down. Here come two rickshaws down the street past us and the front rickshaw was, no person in it but it had looked like barracks bags, who knows what was in it. The second rickshaw behind it had a merchant and in between his feet sitting down there was a bag which was open. He was counting his daily take. And I suspect the rickshaw in front of him had a barracks bag or two full of money also. Of course a bag full of money then wouldn't buy you very much. Just like a dollar today won't do you much here. But then I got, several of us, half a dozen of us or so were sent on detached duty from Kunming to Nanjing China. The shooting had stopped but nobody had signed anything. Either in China or on the Battleship Missouri. So here was a Signal Corps battalion group and we went by the, flew over to Nanjing from Kunming and that's quite a long ways with a two engine plane. Well it was like the old DC-3, that's what it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 47, yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: C-47 whatever. And what we were doing we were carrying drums of gasoline and a radio transmitter and a generator. Gasoline of course would run the generator. And we were to set up the communications. Well we got there in Nanjing and we unloaded all the stuff off the plane onto a flatbed truck. And here was this Chinese driver. And this other guy and I hopped in the back and sat on the drums of gasoline or whatever and we drove up to a movable barricade before you went through the walls of Nanjing into town and there was a Japanese guard, picked up his rifle with a long baronet and pointed. And I thought oh my gosh, if he shoots me and hits me I'm a dead duck. If he shoots and misses and hits the gasoline I'm a dead duck. Don't shoot. Well, he yacked and yacked and yacked with the driver and pretty soon he moved this X type of barricade, moved it over and away we went. We wound up in some four-story hotel in downtown Nanjing. Which I thought was pretty good especially since I had been living in less than accommodations then that for many, many months. Next morning we got up and were told to go down to a certain place down the street for breakfast. And this other guy and I started out, went down there and we were told what the building looked like and we walked along, well that looks like the building. What are the two Japanese guards standing there for? So we started to turn left and all of a sudden they put their rifles across there and made a barricade. We got the message. We backed up and nodded and smiled and went on down the way we were going until we got to another building which looked like the first one. The first building as I was told later was headquarters for the Imperial Japanese Occupation Army. We picked the wrong building to have breakfast. (laughs.) Fortunately we didn't get shot. But we were escorted in to the dining room by some Chinese waiter or whatever you want to call him, and this other guy and I looked back because here we are, we are both sergeants, and sitting around the table, much longer than this dining room table, was admirals and generals and everything, brass. And one woman. The woman was Margaret Bork White. Well, the old army adage, don't fraternize you know, and you don't sit with the brass when eating except in combat conditions or roughing it in beautiful Burma. Well we sat down. We were hungry. The guy showed us in there. So we started eating. And shortly after that in comes some second lieutenant and he almost turned seven shades of white. Enlisted men sitting with the biggest brass you can shake your stick at, both US and British. He went through the roof and drug us into the kitchen. Well I looked back at the brass and Margaret Bork White as we were being shown out and there were several red faces. It had embarrassed the hell out of them. It didn't bother them that we were shown in there, but it embarrassed them when we got heaved out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: But we all outgrew it and lived it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't get to talk to Margaret or hear any of the conversation there?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No. Well, we didn't try to enter in the conversation. Keep your mouth. What you don't say won't come back to haunt you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (laughs.)

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: But anyway never saw them again. But a couple days later, I'll just say let it go at that because I have no idea how many days passed, the Japanese surrendered to the Chinese in a building in Nanjing and you could go and witness the signing if you wished but before you went in you had to sign in on a guest book if you want to call it that. And so a bunch of us, we went in, signed in, went in, sat where were directed up the stairs in the balcony, looked down over them and see what they were doing. Then later on I saw a newsreel of that. There I was standing in line, signing my name. Whatever happened to the newsreel I'll never know. Whether it was shown in this country, I don't know. I don't know who made it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you see that newsreel?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: In Nanjing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh it was while you were still over there.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: While I was still there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it part of like a regular concentration of movies and whatever that you saw before a movie or -

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I can't remember what went with that, before or after. I don't really remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But it was an actual newsreel, do you think that it would be, you know, boxed or kept?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No, I don't think it was a commercial outfit. I think it was Army Signal Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh it might have been an army - Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Or it might have been the Chinese Signal Corps equivalent making it for history.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It may be in the archives somewhere.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. But I ain't looking for it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (laughs.)

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: But there in Nanjing I got to meet an interesting person. He was in the US Embassy staff and went over to his house one night for dinner and he told me what had transpired when he was there prior to World War II. He was there in 1937. Council General. I don't remember what his rank was. We'll let it go at that. And he was on the gun boat Panna and they were on the river. And the Japanese plane came over and sunk them. And I saw that newsreel in this country. And he said the Japanese story and apology, so sorry, didn't know it was US ship, was a bunch of bologna because on top of the pallet house they had the US flag painted as big as the devil. And they are flying one on the stern like you would, it was a US Naval vessel. And he said they were flying so low they could see the face of the Japanese pallets. And they couldn't tell it was a US ship, huh uh. But the terrifying part of the whole thing or another part of the terrifying episode was they escaped off the gunboat as it sank into the river and waded into shore in high reeds and hid there because the Japanese army was coming down the road looking for them, looking for survivors. Maybe they were going to be sure there weren't any. But anyway that was rather interesting. And then I also went to the Sun Yat Sen Memorial. And Sun Yat Sen was man that set up the, over through the last dynasty. Don't ask me if it was the Ming dynasty or what. And Kuomintang party, not communist but - and his, we'll call him his right hand man was Chiang Kai-shek. And his memorial and tomb is top of a hill in Nanjing. And it's about four hundred and some steps up that hill. No elevators. No escalators. The old manual method. And being in the Signal Corps I got elected to escort people up there and take their photograph. So I got to count the steps several times. Don't ask me who it was that had to be photographed. Don't ask. I survived that. And I also talked to some civilians that had been interred by the Japanese when they were living and working in Shanghai when the Japanese took over. And they had some horrors or stories, I'll call it that, to relate. And they said they weren't treated too well until after Tokyo raid. And then they were treated real nice. Japanese guards couldn't do enough for them. Instead of enough to them. And these guys said I guess they were afraid they were going to lose the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is after the Doolittle Raid or something?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah, after the Doolittle Raid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that early in the war?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. So they told me how life had been and how it changed suddenly and then unfortunately went back to what it had been. But after the war ended of course they were released. And after the war ended what did I do? Where did I get transferred? Oh. Shanghai. Now Nanjing was a nice modern city. Occidental as well as oriental, and so was Shanghai. Of course Shanghai was much bigger and had a bigger international section because prior to World War II, Standard Oil, a Texas company, and other US and British companies were there and they had a whole area of Shanghai was called the International Section where they lived and/or worked. But to me coming out of the sticks of Burma, Nanjing looked beautiful and Shanghai did too. And I spent, I don't know how much time I spent in Shanghai or Nanjing for that matter. Fifty, sixty years have passed and memories get kind of dim. But I got to know Shanghai pretty well. The bun which is the waterfront area. And then I got transferred on to attached duty to Chongqing China which was at that time still the capitol. It was the war time capitol because before the Chinese invaded China Nanjing was the capitol. When the Japanese came in the Chinese government moved west to Chongqing. And Chongqing is on, sort of set up like Pittsburg is. Two rivers come in and one goes out. Except they don't rename the rivers there. The Yangtze and some other came together and the Yangtze flowed on to the coast. But here was Chongqing in a similar situation. But it was a strange city in many ways. You could drive down the streets and see pot marks in the multi-story buildings. And those were pot marks created by exploding bombs and/or shrapnel because the Japanese used to come over and bomb them. And I was told the Japanese never had a problem finding Chongqing because all it had to do is turn on the radios in the planes and turn on to the radio station being broadcast out of Chongqing, just hone in on it. Beautiful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The people in Chongqing didn't realize they should stop broadcasting?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I don't know. Well most of them had no control over it and fled.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: In Chongqing the hills were just lots and lots of tunnels dug into it for bomb shelters. And for other reasons later on they used, they used them for other reasons later on. Namely to hide stolen US equipment in. Trucks, jeeps, you name it. Whatever could be moved at times would be liberated shall we say. Or the GI's used to call it moonlight requisitions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any effort to stop that?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. And they tried, US tried to recover some of it but it was an impossible task because the Chinese knew you were coming down this road. What they do they would take the equipment out of this cave and go around and put it in a cave you had already been. It's like trying to squeeze mercury. Tough to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (laughs.)

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: (laughs.) So Chongqing was the last station I had in China. From there I went back to Shanghai and boarded a ship. And I got over into China Burma India in Calcutta, well we sailed on the 11th of January and we got there forty-two days later. It would have been late February I guess. I didn't try to add it up. And I left Shanghai to come back to the states in May of '46. So it was forty-two days going over, but we went the long way see. And it was less days then that coming back because we had a shorter run from Shanghai to Oakland, California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And the first thing I did when we got into Oakland and off the ship and all this, that, and the other and got a little free time we'll call it, we were in a great big warehouse and in there they have a PX. And in the PX they had milk and ice cream which we hadn't had since we left the states and most of us gorged ourselves silly on milk and ice cream. I still eat milk and ice cream but not like that. (laughs.) And from there several days later we were boarded on a troop train and headed to Fort Sam Houston, Texas. And got my walking papers there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: It was real good naturally. Well I had two brothers who had been service, went in before I did and one of them made a career out of it. He stayed for twenty-seven years. That was my oldest brother. And he's still living. The brother between me and my oldest brother, there is three years between each of us, got transferred finally from Dutch Harbor, Alaska to Fort Sill, Oklahoma. But he spent more time overseas then I did in the army. I was in the army about twenty-nine months. He spent almost three years in the Lucian Islands. Never had a pass.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you had not been home all that time too.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No. Once I ended the army, I don't recall if I ever had, maybe I did have a three day pass but once I left Camp Crowder, Missouri heading west, nope, I got to Long Beach and started the journey to the far east and back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a girl back home when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No, I didn't. I was a shy guy I guess. And for that matter after I got out of the service then I took advantage of the GI bill see and I went to college. Well, $65 a month was all I got. And room and board which you paid in advance came to $60. So for the rest of the month I could take my remaining $5 and spend it any way I wanted. But of course this was in the mid 40's and $5 then was a little more than now. But you still couldn't run rampant. Oh I could have a couple of beers and go to show. A show was fifty cents. And I didn't have any money there as a matter of speaking so I didn't have much of a social life in college. I went to a predominantly all male school. There were some females there, not too many. What they were doing, most of them, well some of them, not necessary most, some of them were married to guys going to school. Most of the school at that time of course was GI's, ex-GI's. And some of the women were married to their husbands. That's redundant. Married to their husbands. Anyway, who were full time students. And they might be taking a course in humanities, this, that and the other. And some might were local girls taking courses like that marking time to get to where they wanted to go. So the old adage was when you had a dance there at the School of Mines, Missouri School of Mines of Metallurgy as it was known then, it's now known as the University of Missouri-Rolla. They have a campus at Rolla, St. Louis, Kansas City, and the main was up at -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Columbia.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: -- Columbia, yeah. An old story was well at the dance if the guys parked long enough you could see a female. (laughs.) We outnumbered. I don't know what the ratio was. High. Three thousand students and thirty women. Something like that. But I didn't have any money then so I couldn't socialize there and I never developed any close female relationship with anyone my age. And I didn't until I graduated and moved up here. And that was in 1952. And I've been here since. I have lived here longer then I lived in the town I was born and raised in. But so what.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies overseas?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well, yeah, but I don't know where they are. See we were all replacements and we all got busted apart from, we were sent here, sent there and yonder therefore, so we were chopped up like liver and scattered around. I had one or two guys call me when I got out of the army. One guy and his wife were coming through town. They gave me a call. And we had a conversation of where I lived, half hour or so, while they were relaxing from driving.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Because this was long before the days of interstate. And so the driving wasn't quite as easy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: West 20 or something?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. (laughs.) So I don't have any reunions. I never go to a reunion. I don't know if there is one for that battalion, the last battalion I was in. I was in two different battalions. The first one I went to in Burma, the one that moved into Kunming and then I was detached from there and sent to Nanjing. And we were later then transferred from that battalion, the first battalion, the one I was in with Burma to another outfit in China. So here I was replacement twice. As we all were. So you didn't really have any strong ties. Because I went to Chongqing and some of the other guys went up to Northeast China and some went somewhere else. So we were scattered around. And the only way you could talk to each other was via teletype if they had one where they were. And when I was in Chongqing I worked in the, as a quip-togragher in the message center so I had access to teletype and I could talk to guys in my battalion who were headquartered in Shanghai. Or a conversation or two up in Seng Kow China. But you drift apart.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do much for entertainment over there? You mentioned going to the movies. Anything else you did for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Played cards as every GI does. Shot craps or whatever. Wasted your money one way or another. Didn't have much to waste and so hell, couldn't buy anything just sitting in the jungle, what are you going to buy? There are no stores. In Nanjing, yeah, there was "nightclubs". I don't know what you would call them but I'll label that. You could go, it didn't cost you much for beer or what have you and they would have shows, the local people putting on shows. And went to several restaurants there. And in on place in Nanjing there was three or four of us sitting at a round table right on the edge of a restaurant right on the edge of a dance floor too. And I ordered something cooked in Chinese mushrooms which was a mistake because it was hotter than the hinges of Haitis. And my tongue was on fire. And they didn't serve drinking water. They don't use water in China. At that time they didn't have the purification system. So what did they do? They would boil the water and make tea naturally, which is safe to drink. So I'm dying there for something to cool my tongue down. This waiter brought me a cup of hot tea. It was cooler than my tongue, or it felt like it. But I got over that and was sitting there minding my own business as the saying goes and I turned around, my chair was on the edge of the dance floor at the table. So I turned around to watch them. And here was a small Chinese girl, about ten, twelve, dancing with a, probably her sister, much older and very nice looking. And they went around by us a couple of times. And all of a sudden here they came again. I didn't pay any attention to them, not particularly, I just saw them coming. And as they got opposite me the younger girl pushed her older sister right into my lap. Holly mackerel. I didn't know what to do. Here I'm a foreign national, be careful. Kept my hands to myself. The older girl wound up sitting in my lap and we both looked like red beets. She lost face and the little girl busted out laughing. (laughs.) That's the last I saw of them. They never made another turn around the floor. But all sorts of silly things like that happened to you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any other contacts or chance to deal with the people either in China Burma or India? With the local people?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: In Burma, no, because where we were Bhamo, B-h-a-m-o, it had been blasted off the face of the earth because of artillery siege and the 10th Air Force bombing raids. And I got to meet some people in Calcutta and Nanjing and some in Shanghai. And it was very interesting from one standpoint. For instance there was one place in Calcutta you walked down the street and you keep looking at it it looks like the slums of the world. Here is these houses with big high stone wall fences and a gate. Well we went through the gate as we were instructed, went into the house, but once you got in that gate everything changed. It was no longer a slum. High class. Well, I did meet one interesting person in Chongqing. Don't ask me how. But we were invited out to his house. He was a merchant. He lived outside of town. And we were invited to his house for dinner. You walked into his house and it was solid marble walls and floors. I dreamt I dwelt in marble halls, that came to mind. And he served us some sumptuous meal. I don't remember what it was. But one of them I do remember. It was big around, the old fashioned jawbreaker. Small golf ball or maybe bigger. And it had a grape candy, not a hard candy but a soft candy type of coating all around it. Well pick it up and eat it. Tasted good. I had several of them. Later found out what it was. Candied grasshoppers. So the old adage which you ought to follow if you're eating in a restaurant in the Orient, if you don't know what it is, don't ask. It might be all right if you're in a restaurant but if you're in a home don't ask because you'd lose face and cause the host to be embarrassed. So eat it or don't, but don't ask. Because if you ask you may not want to eat it. But I survived all of that stuff. I guess you might say if I survived some of the army cooking I could survive most anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think of the army food?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well, from time to time it was pretty good and from time to time it wasn't. When I was in Burma our cooks were can openers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not even heating it up?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well, yes. Of course when we were on the road on a run everything was cold. Except when we went from Bhamo up to Kunming, we were on that road so long that we had army, one six by had army kitchens in it. And they cooked some of the meals for us. But a lot of times we'd do it because we were on a stretch of so long. One day the first truck took off about daybreak, 6 o'clock in the morning I'll say. And the truck, convoy I mean was about a hundred and ten trucks. And the last truck that pulled in to our stop that night pulled in at 3 o'clock in the morning. (laughs.) So you ate a lot of cold good old fashioned C-rations or K-rations. And there was one place in Nanjing in our place in that hotel we were at that the cooking was excellent. (end of track one) So I ate it. Everybody did. They wanted more and more. What the guy had done is taken one of these great big cans that the army had stuff in and laced it. And he let it ferment, that cut up fruit, for several days. That was hard to take. We practically inhaled it when we found out what it was. Yeah, you know, everything was, being worse was to have was good and that's why we ate it. Nobody complained to him about dessert or the cooking. It was good food. That's probably the best food I had in the army. I don't mean because of the dessert, but there was by a professional chef. And you know the army does a lot of pick-up stuff. What the hell. They can just grab everybody, you do this, you do that, square peg in a round hole, too bad, how sad, you're dead. For some reason I wound up in what I wanted to do, in the Signal Corps see. Like I said I think my father pulled strings. He did for my brother. My oldest brother made twenty-seven years, a career out of twenty-seven years. He transferred out of the anti-aircraft into the Air Corps, the Army Air Corps at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And then they became Air Force. But anyway he married and had a couple, two or three children. And he was stationed at Wright Patterson. And they transferred he and his family to Spain back and forth a couple of times. Well he got tired of that and one daughter died over there of pneumonia and so that kind of soured him. And so he got more orders one time back at Dayton, Wright Patterson to go back to Europe. And he called up my father and he says I'm tired of this. Can you get these orders repealed? Shortly thereafter the orders were cancelled. My father called one of his connections. I think it was one of the US Senators that he knew personally. And that ended that. Well everything went fine until the Air Corps renigged and cut new orders to go back to Europe. My brother told them I ain't going. I'm resigning right now. That was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was your father a businessman or a politician?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: He was a businessman and a politician. He was not an elected politician per se. He wasn't an alderman or councilman or whatever you want to call them. He dealt with lawyers. He was a printer and dealt with lawyers. And you know what the makeup of most legislative bodies are, lawyers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And so he knew Tom, Dick, and Harry. And they done a lot of favors for him. And he also headed up the election in that county like Janet Claire or whatever, well like the woman -

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Like the woman here in Lake County. He was head of the elections. And he did that for thirty-eight years in the solid south which was democrat at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And he was republican. The governor re-appointed him, every governor that came in and out always re-appointed him so he knew a lot of people because of that too and vice versa. And so he had connections. Sort of like a plumber you might say. And he used them from time to time but very carefully.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And so I think he pulled strings when I was just about to get drafted, and when my oldest brother said he'd had it, didn't want to go back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you when the atomic bombs were dropped?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: When in the hell was that dropped?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nanjing or Chongqing?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I don't remember. Oh it was August?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be August.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Where was I? I wasn't in Shanghai. I must have been in Chongqing. My guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing that news and comprehending what that was all about?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I didn't quite understand what it was all about. I don't remember the wording I heard on the radio, but it just didn't sink in. What is an atomic bomb? Ninety-nine percent of us at that time didn't understand it either I guess. I didn't. But we could hear it, hear all sorts of news see because being in the Signal Corps we had all sorts of radio equipment. In fact at Chongqing we could broadcast non-stop from Chongqing to Honolulu. It was a big powerful transmitter. And after the war was over while we still had that transmitter and were still using it, we wouldn't try to broadcast that far. We'd broadcast to Shanghai and they would then relay it. You wouldn't lose strength. Because sometimes the signal would drift, especially if you got suns kicking up sun spots.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: It may go out to never and never get it received. But after the war is over, as I said we kept that transmitter and for a while we had a disc jockey show. We would play certain music and beam it of course heading west and ask if you heard it, this music, give us the name of it, what time you heard it and where you heard it. And we got some back from we'll say San Jose, California. Postcards. And they later dismantled the transmitter because we were breaking down the station getting ready to close it down. But this was back in the vacuum tube days. The big powerful tubes, one to an orange crate, big.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah. Well it was over a fifty thousand watt station. And when they took all the tubes off and stripped the whole thing down and put the chasse on the back of an army six by they had to take the vertical sides off. And it overhung. And coming down this old hand-laid stone street, little wider than this, not as wide as this room, here is an arch and they had to go through that arch with that big chasse sitting on it and it had three guys directing the driver. One to look overhead because it had an arch, one for this side, and one for that side. They got by about that much. It must have been fun and games taking it up there too. But there was interesting things like that that took place. It wasn't all nitty gritty. There were times.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say - Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I said there were times it wasn't all, wasn't so "funny".

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any of those times you'd like to share?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No. I lucked out. By that I mean I didn't get to shoot anybody and nobody shot at me and I don't regret it. I got there just after as it turned out, probably every time. But like I said don't knock it. Quit while you're ahead or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in Nanjing between the bombs and the signing of the treaty? Is that what you said?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: I was in Chongqing at the atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Chongqing.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And Nanjing, got there in late August.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that's -

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Maybe that's where I heard about the bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that's where the Japanese were guarding the Imperial Headquarters.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah, that was the headquarters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was basically like a cease fire between the bombs and the signing of the treaty.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there tension between the allies and the Japanese people there?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: You couldn't tell it. Well at least I couldn't say because I didn't see many of them. We were told to stand clear - Oh we were disarmed before we got into the city. They didn't want any hot headed GI to pop off a gun because we were so oddly numbered, thousands upon thousands to one you might say. They wanted the cease fire to hold together. So we were without any means of defense or offense except for some GI's big mouth. (laughs.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that pretty scary?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Oh it was. It was kind of, you got used to it pretty soon, but like I said that first morning this other guy and I went for breakfast it was pretty scary. But we had sense enough not to say anything and just kept on going. But the two buildings looked pretty similar. But the Japanese moved out after a short period of time after they signed the peace treaty in Chongqing. The Japanese Army of Occupation for China signed there in Nanjing and left. They had been disarmed. All their rifles and samari swords, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera were taken away. And where they went, who knows. But then later on of course came the allied acceptance of the surrender on the Missouri which is now docked in Honolulu.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Right up from the Arizona.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I went to see that out there years ago.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War II do any other particularly vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well - Well, I told you about that, rumors that the war was over and it wasn't and I was six blocks from home when the guy woke me up. (laughs.) Murder went running through my mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't have that dream again, huh?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: No. And the funny rickshaws full of money, breakfast with the brass in Nanjing. Shanghai was nice and then to Chongqing. I think I liked Nanjing better. Maybe because of the fact it was the first place of western civilization that I had seen after I left Calcutta. And Calcutta was a strange area. It's an aged city by US standards. And the funny thing about Calcutta was at a stop signal, traffic light, you could see all modes of transportation. There were people on foot, automobiles, taxi cabs or what. Sort of like the wonderful one horse shay carriages and rickshaws. All modes of transportation lined up at the stoplight. But it was also a dirty city. Cholera ran rampant and before we left the states we got all sorts of shots for Bubonic plague, cholera, most everything, and booster shots for tetanus. The only shot we didn't get was yellow fever because it's not predominant over there. But we got everything else. In Calcutta their sanitary system leaves a little to be desired just as it does in Chongqing, but cholera running rampant the people keel over from death from cholera right down town in the big commercial area. For instance if you were downtown on a public square in Cleveland in front of what, it wouldn't be, Dillard's I guess now or it used to be Higbey's and May Company and all that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Here we were walking down the street one day in the best section of Calcutta and laying across the sidewalk was a body. People just stepped over him, kept going. But sooner or later trucks would come by and pick him and they had body disposal trucks like they have garbage disposal here. And you'd see all sorts of deformities. Some of them I think people deformed themselves to try to induce you to give them money begging. But the sanitation system left a lot to be desired. One of the stipulations the army gave us when we first got to Calcutta was you can buy any fruit you want, apples, pears, whatever, bananas, but if the skin is broken do not eat it. You could get cholera. Well here you get an apple from the grocery store and you get home you find the skin is nicked a little bit, so what, take a knife and wack it out, go about your business, eat it. Not over there. You weren't supposed. Well if somebody did and didn't get sick, I don't know, I never tried it. I figured they knew more about it then I did. Why stretch my luck. But I never want to go back to Chongqing. I had a choice, chance that is when I was still working. My boss called me in, I was an engineer and we did control systems for utilities basically. Naval vessels too and just control for whoever or whatever. Most of my work was public utilities like CEI, Detroit, anyway he called me in the office one day and he had a stack of specifications on his desk and said we've got a job here for a national thermal power corporation of India. Do you know anybody that would like to go to India? And I said I'll tell you who's not going, just like that. He got the message. I think what he was trying to do is get me to agree to take the job. But having been to beautiful downtown Calcutta, "beautiful", I wanted no more to do with it. And it would have been a free trip. I didn't want anything to do with it. I went back to Shanghai once, not as an employee, after I retired my wife and I went to Shanghai and China that is a couple of years ago and we went to Bashing, Sheon where the taracar warriors are, and Shanghai. Now I wanted to see Shanghai because fifty-five years had passed and I wanted to see what it looked like. It had changed like you might as well expect. Because when I first got there in the fall of '45 about a million and a half people. When I sailed out of there the following May to come back to the states it was up to about three million because the people had come back in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: The Japanese were gone. They had come back in. When my wife and I were over there two years ago this population of Shanghai had only grown to about fourteen million.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And ten million bicycles. (laughs.) But it was an interesting city. I was glad to get back to see it, how much it had changed. And the Bund no longer is decrepit as it was then. There is a bunch of junk sailing vessels tied up to it and helter skelter. Now it's big a big park area and that Bund runs a long way in Shanghai, the water front. And Nanjing Road was one of the main thoroughfares that I usually travelled when I was there in the military. In my opinion it's not as beautiful as it was because right now on every light fixture, both sides of the street, hang a big sign that says Pepsi Cola for miles. (laughs.) Commercialism. But Shanghai was an interesting city too, and like I said I think Nanjing sticks in my mind basically if for no other reason because of the first city of the style in which you and I are used to. It was basically occidental because of commerce.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Money still speaks. No matter what the currency is it talks. (laughs.) But I don't know that I would really want to live in Shanghai or Beijing. Just too much humanity. I wouldn't want to live in New York or Los Angeles. And I don't live in Cleveland although Cleveland is not hardly anywhere as big as either of those cities are. When I came to Cleveland in '52 I worked in the suburb and I lived in the suburb all my life since I've been here. And I came in '52 so what, fifty-one, fifty-two years or thereabouts. Lived and worked in suburbs. And I don't miss having to drive down town especially when they were re-doing the shore way, you know, the lanes had been repaired. The two on the right. Come back the next day and the barrels had been moved to the other side. To heck with that mess. But I don't know, I think I have given you most of the highlights.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think you have covered it?

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Well, the hammock broke, I told you about that, three runs on the Burma Road, two meals a day on the troop ship unless I was in working detail and I volunteered so I could eat three meals. The rumors about the war ending, Kunming, rickshaw full of money, Nanjing, breakfast with the brass, hang out in Chongqing, finally I got home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (laughs.)

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And guess what, at Fort Sam Houston when I was being interviewed or maybe you want to call it being de-briefed like everyone was, the guy sitting across the table from me asked me if I wanted to join the reserves. I busted out laughing. And he said in a rather hostile tone what's so funny. And I thought to myself you better shut up or you won't get out. (laughs.) And I'm glad I didn't join the reserves because being in the Signal Corps you know what happened when Korea started, I would have been right over there. And I didn't want anything to do with it, the military. I was tired of it. One brother stayed in for twenty-seven years. The other one stayed in only as long as they kept him. That was my story too. But to each his own.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Oh there is one other thing that just came to my mind. Aboard that transport, army transport, we were in the South Pacific somewhere, well had nothing to do so some of the guys had a good idea. And it was. I got a group of different ones putting on skits, doing this, that and the other, singing songs, and everything went great until four guys got up, formed a quartet and sang a song. Their song was an extract from Anton Dvorak's New World Symphony and the name of the excerpt was titled Going Home. We didn't know where we were going, but we knew where we weren't going. They didn't get much applause. Every time I hear that song I'm back on that troop transport. Funny how the mind does things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: And why I didn't write it down on my crib sheet, I don't know, just didn't occur to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm still recording so I have it.

sp.speaker: Eugene M. Laubach
sp.p: Okay. I think I hit the highlights or the low lights or half way in between. Well, I appreciate the opportunity.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Thank you. You're done. (end of track two)
